title: Qualcomm to Cut Jobs Worldwide in Performance-Focused Layoffs From November
excerpt: CEO Cristiano Amon told staff in a memo reviewed by Reuters that cuts following annual reviews will begin with notifications in November, with no headcount disclosed.
body:
• Qualcomm will cut jobs globally in a performance-focused reduction after its annual employee reviews, with notifications set to begin in November, according to a memo from CEO Cristiano Amon reviewed by Reuters.
  • The memo did not state how many of Qualcomm's roughly 52,000 employees will be affected, and the company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
  • Amon said decisions will weigh business priorities, organisational needs, skills and expertise, and are aimed at addressing areas where the company has consistently fallen short of expectations.
  • For employees: the only confirmed timeline is notifications from November — no site, role or country breakdown has been disclosed, so claims about specific offices, including in India, are not supported by the memo as reported.

Qualcomm will cut jobs across its global workforce in a "performance-focused reduction" following its annual employee reviews, chief executive Cristiano Amon told staff in a memo on Monday reviewed by Reuters, with notifications set to begin in November.

The cuts are part of an effort to build "a stronger performance culture" and address situations where the company "has consistently fallen short of expectations," Amon said, according to reports by The Hindu BusinessLine and Mint. The memo did not say how many jobs would be affected, and Reuters could not immediately determine the scale of the cuts. Qualcomm did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

"We must have the right people in the right roles so they can perform at their best and the company can continue to succeed."

— Cristiano Amon, Chief Executive, Qualcomm

What the memo says

Amon said business priorities, organisational needs, skills and expertise would be considered in making the cuts. "As we have expanded the business, so have the competencies and skills we require," he wrote. Qualcomm had about 52,000 employees globally as of September last year, most of them full-time, and its financial year typically ends in late September — the point at which the annual review cycle that triggered this round concludes.

The framing matters. Qualcomm is describing this round as performance-based, tied to individual reviews, rather than as a restructuring of a named division or a cost-cutting programme with a published headcount target. No severance terms, affected functions or locations were disclosed in the memo as reported.

Pressure on the handset business

Qualcomm, one of the world's biggest smartphone chipmakers, has been hit this year by a slump in consumer electronics sales as soaring memory prices weigh on demand in key markets. Its shares have risen just 1.5% in 2026, compared with gains of more than 12% for the benchmark S&P 500 and nearly 60% for the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index.

In its latest earnings report in late July, Qualcomm forecast quarterly profit below estimates and said revenue from Apple products would decline faster than expected. Apple has been moving its modem business in-house, eroding a long-standing Qualcomm revenue stream.

The pivot beyond smartphones

Against that pressure, Qualcomm has signalled that growth in data-centre and other non-handset businesses would more than offset the lost Apple revenue by fiscal 2027. The company expects the majority of its chip sales to come from businesses other than smartphones in fiscal 2027 as it expands into the fast-growing artificial intelligence data-centre market.

That pivot helps explain the memo's emphasis on skills. A company shifting its centre of gravity from handset modems toward data-centre silicon needs a different mix of engineering expertise, and Amon's language — right people, right roles — points to reallocation as well as reduction.

What happens next

Notifications begin in November, which is when the actual scale — numbers, functions and countries — will become visible, likely through local filings and employee reports rather than a single company announcement. Until then, the confirmed facts are narrow: a global, performance-linked reduction, decided after annual reviews, with no published total. For Qualcomm's large engineering workforce in India and elsewhere, the November notifications, not speculation about sites or roles, will be the first reliable signal of who is affected.
